question.:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ over the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](images/0a/0a1de805051eff4ea82b4eefb7bb113c724b3d4e7304704831b6294ee4e4d674.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}2{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{81}{4}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2$ and the line $y=x+2,$ as shown above. What is
$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $(-1,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=x+2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2 \\ r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](images/b9/b9c2cd48302ef8d4e2d5e65a56d19506600c5e6552a4d9a1ef7d578a09a21557.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\le r\le 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{2/(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{2/(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,3u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-3\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(-7u+4v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-x}_{P},\,\underbrace{-y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{xy(2x+y)}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨1,\,0,\,y⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{1}_{P},\,\underbrace{0}_{Q},\,\underbrace{y}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{P},\,\underbrace{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}_{Q},\,\underbrace{1}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,{cos}^{2}⁡(xy),\,1⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot \left(\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}\right)-({cos}^{2}⁡(xy))\cdot \left(\frac{x}{{cos}^{2}⁡(xy)}\right)+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-x+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(-y-x+1)\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-xy+y]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-{x}^{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x)\,dx \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,x={t}^{2},$ and $y=t,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=⟨0,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨2,0,1⟩.$ Find $a\times b.$

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =((0)(1)-(0)(3))i-((0)(1)-(2)(3))j+((0)(0)-(2)(0))k \\  & =(0-0)i-(0-6)j+(0-0)k \\  & =6j.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ x & 2 & 3 \\ 2x & 5 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}x & 3 \\ 2x & 2\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}x & 2 \\ 2x & 5\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(4-15)i-(2x-6x)j+(5x-4x)k \\  & =⟨-11,4x,x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{(-11)^{2}+(4x)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{121+16{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17{x}^{2}+121}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 4.$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2(t+1),\,y=4{t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=8t.
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
8t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Note that ${x}^{′}(0)=2\ne 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t=0,$ the tangent to the curve is horizontal.

$$
x=3{t}^{2}-2t,\,y={t}^{2}-1,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=2.$

We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6t-2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t}{6t-2}=\frac{t}{3t-1}.
$$

At the point where $t=2$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2}{3(2)-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{6-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
